title: Even Black Friday Will Be More Expensive Than Usual
gist: Black Friday 2026 deals are expected to be weaker as an AI-driven memory (RAM) crisis and the war in Iran push up prices, especially for memory-heavy electronics like PCs, tablets, smartphones and consoles; IDC expects elevated pricing into 2027–2028, Amazon has raised device prices, and manufacturers are increasingly buying back units to sell as refurbished.

themes.theme: AI memory crisis driving consumer electronics inflation

insights.claim: Prices for many products, especially consumer electronics like smartphones and gaming consoles, have risen as the global economy contends with the AI industry's memory crisis and the ongoing war in Iran.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: AI datacenter demand for memory is spilling into consumer device pricing, benefiting memory makers and squeezing device margins/demand.

insights.claim: IDC's Jitesh Ubrani expects device prices to keep rising well into 2027 and possibly 2028, with PCs and tablets the hardest hit.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Multi-year elevated memory pricing supports memory supplier earnings while pressuring PC/tablet unit volumes.
insights.quote: Things are getting more expensive, and they'll probably continue to get more expensive well into 2027, maybe even 2028

insights.claim: Black Friday deals will likely be weakest on memory-intensive products, while gadgets less reliant on RAM, such as robot vacuums and headphones, may see better prices.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Memory content per device is a useful lens for which consumer hardware categories face margin or demand pressure.
insights.locator: While many sales have already begun

insights.claim: Amazon has raised prices on its latest Kindles, tablets, and Echo speakers, making its upcoming sales on those devices likely less impressive than in prior years.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Even the largest retailer is passing through component cost inflation on its own hardware.

insights.claim: Consumer advocate Edgar Dworsky predicts laptops, desktops, and SSDs will still be discounted on Black Friday but not nearly as low as previous years because of high memory prices.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Shallower discounts imply weaker holiday unit volumes for PC and storage vendors.
insights.quote: Because of high memory prices, laptops, desktops, and SSDs will still be on sale

insights.claim: Amid economic turmoil, companies have been adept at passing additional costs to consumers, making Black Friday good mainly for the sellers who set the prices.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Suggests retailers and brands retain pricing power, protecting margins despite input cost increases.
insights.locator: What Black Friday will be good for

insights.claim: IDC's Ubrani advises consumers to buy the most performance they can afford now because elevated pricing is expected to persist for years.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: May pull forward demand and shift mix toward higher-spec devices in the near term.
insights.quote: We're going to face elevated pricing for years.
insights.locator: “They should be purchasing the most amount

insights.claim: Some device manufacturers are buying back their own products from resellers like BStock Solutions to refurbish and sell as authorized refurbished or certified renewed units, filling gaps in the budget phone market.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Growth of OEM-run refurbished channels is a second-order effect of component inflation and a tailwind for secondary-market players.
insights.quote: They're trying to get anything and everything back.

insights.claim: Edgar Dworsky warns that advertised savings do not necessarily mean a good deal and recommends tracking prices with price-history tools like CamelCamelCamel or Chrome's built-in tracker.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Price-history transparency tools constrain retailers' ability to inflate claimed discounts.
